subtopic_detail: Abrupt onset of complex tic like movements over two days in a seventeen year old with no childhood history
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar assessing a 17 year old student whose movements began over two days six weeks ago and have escalated since. She flings both arms outwards, slaps her own sternum, and shouts obscene phrases in an accent that is not her own.

Her mother says the phrases are word for word the ones used by a creator she watches for several hours each night on a video sharing platform. The movements are continuous through the consultation, worsen markedly when the medical students enter, and stop entirely for around a minute when you ask her to copy a two handed tapping rhythm. She reports no warning sensation before a movement and says she cannot hold them back even briefly. She had no tics as a child, and an anxiety disorder was diagnosed a year ago.

data_table.Examination: Complex bilateral flinging movements with self striking, entrainment of the movements to an imposed tapping rhythm, no stereotyped simple motor tics, normal tone power and reflexes, no chorea
data_table.Investigations: Copper studies and caeruloplasmin within normal limits, thyroid stimulating hormone 1.6 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), full blood count and electrolytes within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start aripiprazole and review the frequency of the movements in four weeks
options.rationale: Dopamine blocking agents are first line for tics of Tourette syndrome, and that is the diagnosis being assumed, but the features here run against it: onset in adolescence over two days, complex movements from the outset, absent premonitory urge, no capacity for suppression and entrainment on distraction. Treating with an antipsychotic exposes her to weight gain and akathisia for no expected benefit. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology

options.text: Explain the positive diagnosis and refer for tailored psychological therapy
options.rationale: Abrupt onset, absence of a premonitory urge, inability to suppress, entrainment to an imposed rhythm, worsening under observation and phrases copied from media exposure are positive signs of a functional movement disorder rather than diagnostic exclusions. Explaining the mechanism as a genuine disorder of movement control that is reversible, rather than describing what she does not have, is itself the first and most effective step of treatment. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

options.text: Start clonidine and review the frequency of the movements in four weeks
options.rationale: Clonidine is used for tics with comorbid attention deficit hyperactivity disorder and has a gentler adverse effect profile than antipsychotics, but it shares the same wrong premise as the other drug option and adds sedation and postural hypotension in a young woman who drives. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and review her with the result
options.rationale: Imaging is appropriate when the examination is abnormal in other domains or the movements are unilateral or fixed, and hers are not, with normal tone, power, reflexes and no chorea. Investigating to exclude rather than diagnosing positively prolongs uncertainty, and a normal scan rarely reassures a patient who has been told the cause is unknown. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

options.text: Refer for botulinum toxin injection to the most affected muscle groups
options.rationale: Botulinum toxin is used for focal dystonia and for a small number of severe, localised and injurious tics, whereas her movements are generalised, variable and change from consultation to consultation. Injecting a shifting pattern of muscles cannot work and reinforces a structural explanation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology

explanation.summary: Functional tic like behaviours rose sharply among adolescent girls from 2020 and are now a common presentation to paediatric and neurology clinics, frequently in patients with heavy exposure to social media content featuring tics. They are distinguished from Tourette syndrome by abrupt onset after childhood rather than gradual onset between five and seven years, complex rather than simple movements from the beginning, absence of the premonitory urge that patients with tics describe vividly, absence of any suppressibility, a rostrocaudal pattern that does not fit the usual face to limb progression, and entrainment or distractibility on examination. Coprolalia is common in the functional group and rare in Tourette syndrome, which inverts the usual assumption. Treatment is a clear positive explanation, reduction of the reinforcing exposure, and a tailored psychological therapy addressing the frequently comorbid anxiety, with dopamine blocking drugs specifically unhelpful. Outcomes are good when the diagnosis is delivered confidently and early, and poor when the patient is investigated repeatedly and left without an explanation.
key_points: Abrupt adolescent onset with complex movements argues against Tourette syndrome
Absent premonitory urge and absent suppressibility are key positive discriminators
Entrainment to an imposed rhythm is a positive functional sign, not an exclusion
Coprolalia is common in functional presentations and rare in Tourette syndrome
Antipsychotics and botulinum toxin are ineffective and reinforce the wrong model
explanation.pearls: Ask specifically whether there is a build up of tension or an itch like sensation relieved by performing the movement: that premonitory urge is reported by over ninety per cent of adolescents with Tourette syndrome and almost never in functional tic like behaviours, and a single clear negative answer is worth more than a magnetic resonance scan.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists
Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne clinical practice guideline

subtopic_detail: Nightmares and hypervigilance in a man on a bridging visa awaiting a protection decision with no income
stem:
You are the general practitioner at a community health service seeing a 34 year old man who arrived by boat six years ago and has been on a bridging visa for three years. A professional interpreter attends in person at his request.

He describes nightmares most nights, waking sweating, intrusive daytime memories of being beaten in custody in his home country, startling at doors closing, and avoiding the news. He has no work rights at present, is sleeping on a friend's couch after being asked to leave his room, and has not seen his wife and daughter for six years. His protection application is awaiting a decision and he says he cannot think past it. He denies thoughts of suicide, has no psychotic symptoms and asks you for sleeping tablets so that he can rest.

data_table.Examination: Guarded and watchful, startles when the door closes, well oriented, no psychotic features, healed scarring over both shins
data_table.Investigations: Vitamin D 38 nmol/L (50-150), haemoglobin 141 g/L (130-175), thyroid stimulating hormone 2.3 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), electrolytes within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start diazepam at night and review his sleep in two weeks with the interpreter
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines are specifically discouraged in post-traumatic stress disorder because they do not improve core symptoms, impair the extinction learning on which trauma focused therapy depends, and carry dependence risk in a population with high rates of chronic distress. Meeting the request as made would feel responsive and would set treatment back. (Source: Phoenix Australia: Australian guidelines for the treatment of post-traumatic stress disorder)
source_refs: Phoenix Australia: Australian guidelines for the treatment of post-traumatic stress disorder

options.text: Begin trauma focused exposure therapy at weekly sessions without further delay
options.rationale: Trauma focused therapy is the first line treatment for this disorder and will be the centre of his care, but it works on the premise that the danger is in the past, and he faces an unresolved removal decision, housing loss and separation from his family. Starting exposure work before those are stabilised commonly leads to dropout and deterioration. (Source: Phoenix Australia: Australian guidelines for the treatment of post-traumatic stress disorder)
source_refs: Phoenix Australia: Australian guidelines for the treatment of post-traumatic stress disorder

options.text: Start mirtazapine at night and review his sleep in two weeks with the interpreter
options.rationale: Antidepressants are a reasonable second line option for this disorder when psychological treatment is unavailable or declined, but prescribing alone as the response to a presentation dominated by homelessness, destitution and an unresolved visa leaves the drivers of the distress untouched. Medication may still be added once the social situation is addressed. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic

options.text: Defer any mental health treatment until his visa application has been decided
options.rationale: Waiting for legal resolution can mean waiting years and abandons him during the period of greatest risk, and stabilisation work, sleep interventions and practical support are all deliverable now. The correct answer sequences treatment rather than withholding it. (Source: Victorian Foundation for Survivors of Torture)
source_refs: Victorian Foundation for Survivors of Torture

options.text: Refer to a specialist torture and trauma service and address housing and income
options.rationale: Survivors of torture with ongoing insecurity are treated in phases, beginning with safety, stabilisation and the practical determinants that sustain the hyperarousal, delivered by a service with interpreters and expertise in the medico-legal context, before trauma processing work begins. Housing, income support and assistance with the visa process are clinical interventions in this population rather than social extras. (Source: Victorian Foundation for Survivors of Torture)
source_refs: Victorian Foundation for Survivors of Torture

explanation.summary: Rates of post-traumatic stress disorder and depression in people seeking asylum in Australia are several times those of the general population, and the strongest predictors of ongoing symptoms are not the severity of past torture but the current post-migration living difficulties: visa insecurity, family separation, lack of work rights, and unstable housing. That finding is what drives the phased treatment model, in which safety, stabilisation, sleep, pain and the practical determinants are addressed first, and trauma focused processing follows once the environment is stable enough to support it. Specialist torture and trauma services exist in every state and territory and provide counselling, complex case work, medico-legal reports and interpreter services at no cost. Benzodiazepines are avoided, and where medication is needed a serotonergic antidepressant is preferred. A professional interpreter is used rather than a family member or bilingual friend, both for accuracy and because disclosure of torture and sexual violence is inhibited when the interpreter belongs to the patient's community.
key_points: Post-migration living difficulties predict symptom persistence more strongly than past trauma
Phased treatment puts safety and stabilisation before trauma processing
Specialist torture and trauma services are free and available in every state
Benzodiazepines impair extinction learning and are avoided in this disorder
Use a professional interpreter rather than a family member or community friend
explanation.pearls: Ask about the visa stage explicitly at every visit: the weeks around a refusal or a tribunal hearing carry a sharp rise in self harm in this population, and knowing the date of a pending decision lets you schedule a review for that week rather than discovering the deterioration afterwards.

sources.label: Victorian Foundation for Survivors of Torture
Phoenix Australia: Australian guidelines for the treatment of post-traumatic stress disorder

subtopic_detail: A written advance statement naming a preferred antipsychotic during a later manic relapse under compulsory treatment
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar on call. A 38 year old carpenter with bipolar disorder has been admitted as an involuntary patient. He has not slept for four nights, is speaking continuously, has spent most of his savings in two days and is refusing food, fluids and all medication.

Eight months ago, while well and in the company of his case manager, he completed and signed a written advance statement. It records that he does not want olanzapine because of the 18 kg he gained on it after his last admission, that he would accept aripiprazole, and that his sister is his nominated support person. There is no clinical reason in his file why aripiprazole would be unsuitable, and it is available on the ward. His sister has not yet been contacted.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118 beats per minute, blood pressure 142/84 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 37.2 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Continuous pressured speech, flight of ideas, grandiose content, dry mucous membranes, no focal neurological signs
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 146 mmol/L (135-145), creatinine 102 micromol/L (60-110), creatine kinase 380 units/L (40-200), urine drug screen negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate course of action?

options.text: Treat with the agent he nominated in the statement and inform his nominated person
options.rationale: Australian mental health legislation requires the treating team to make reasonable efforts to give effect to a valid advance statement of preferences and to involve the nominated support person, and here the stated preference is clinically appropriate and available, so there is no ground to depart from it. Honouring a preference made while well is also the intervention most likely to preserve engagement after this admission. (Source: Victorian Mental Health and Wellbeing Act principles)
source_refs: Victorian Mental Health and Wellbeing Act principles

options.text: Treat with olanzapine because his advance statement is not binding while he is unwell
options.rationale: It is true that a statement of preferences is not absolutely binding in the way a refusal of physical treatment by a competent adult is, but that is not permission to ignore it; the obligation to make reasonable efforts to comply survives the loss of capacity, which is the entire point of writing it in advance. (Source: Victorian Mental Health and Wellbeing Act principles)
source_refs: Victorian Mental Health and Wellbeing Act principles

options.text: Apply to the tribunal for a ruling before giving any antipsychotic medication to him
options.rationale: The tribunal reviews compulsory treatment orders and hears applications about them, but it does not need to authorise a routine treatment decision that is already within the authorised psychiatrist's power, and his sodium, pulse and creatine kinase mean days of delay carry real physical risk. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

options.text: Withhold all antipsychotic medication because he is currently refusing all treatment
options.rationale: Current refusal is why he is under a compulsory order in the first place, and withholding treatment in a patient who is four nights without sleep, hypernatraemic and not drinking risks delirium, rhabdomyolysis and physical collapse. Refusal by a patient without capacity does not have the same standing as a considered advance refusal. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

options.text: Treat with olanzapine and record written reasons for departing from the statement
options.rationale: Documenting written reasons is exactly what the legislation requires when a preference must be overridden, so this option is procedurally correct but substantively wrong: departure is permitted when the preference is not clinically appropriate or not available, and here the nominated drug is both. The difference from the correct answer is whether any valid reason to depart exists. (Source: Victorian Mental Health and Wellbeing Act principles)
source_refs: Victorian Mental Health and Wellbeing Act principles

explanation.summary: Advance statements of preferences are a central mechanism of supported decision making in contemporary Australian mental health legislation, allowing a person to record, while well, what treatment they would and would not want during a future episode of illness. They are not identical to an advance care directive refusing physical treatment, which binds absolutely; a mental health statement of preferences must be given effect where reasonably possible, and where it is departed from the authorised psychiatrist must record written reasons and notify the patient and their nominated support person. Nominated support persons have statutory rights to be informed and to be involved in decisions, and a failure to contact them is one of the commonest procedural errors on an after hours admission. Honouring a stated medication preference that is clinically reasonable costs nothing and substantially improves the therapeutic relationship after discharge, whereas overriding it confirms the belief that the statement was pointless. Weight gain on olanzapine is not a trivial objection: it is the commonest reason patients discontinue treatment and it carries real cardiometabolic consequences.
key_points: A statement of preferences must be given effect where reasonably possible
Departure requires written reasons and notification of the patient and nominated person
Nominated support persons have statutory rights to be informed and involved
Compulsory status does not remove the obligation to follow stated preferences
A clinically appropriate and available preferred drug leaves no ground to depart
explanation.pearls: Check the sodium and creatine kinase in acute mania before anything else: several days without sleeping, eating or drinking produces dehydration, hypernatraemia and rising creatine kinase from sustained motor activity, and these physical consequences, not the psychiatric symptoms, are what make a delay of days genuinely dangerous.

sources.label: Victorian Mental Health and Wellbeing Act principles
Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

subtopic_detail: A fifth emergency presentation this year with superficial forearm cuts after a relationship ended
stem:
You are the emergency registrar seeing a 24 year old woman who arrived at eleven at night with parallel superficial cuts to the left forearm made with a craft knife after her partner ended their relationship. None require suturing and there is no tendon or nerve involvement.

This is her fifth presentation in twelve months. She has been attending a dialectical behaviour therapy programme for five months and her next skills group is in three days; her therapist's crisis plan is scanned into the record and names an after hours number and two agreed strategies. She is not intoxicated and her observations are normal. Over the ninety minutes since arrival she has become notably calmer, has eaten a sandwich and now says she does not want to die and has no plan. She asks to be admitted so that she will be safe. Her two previous admissions were both complicated by escalating self injury on the ward.

data_table.Examination: Six superficial parallel forearm lacerations with no deep structure involvement, settled and coherent, no depressive psychomotor change, no psychotic features
data_table.Investigations: Breath alcohol zero, paracetamol not detected, full blood count and electrolytes within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate disposition?

options.text: Admit her overnight to the short stay unit and review her with the team tomorrow
options.rationale: A short stay admission looks like a compromise but still removes her from the environment in which the skills are meant to be used, and it teaches that distress at eleven at night is resolved by a bed. It is appropriate when intoxication, a medical issue or genuine uncertainty about intent needs a few hours to settle. (Source: National Health and Medical Research Council: Clinical practice guideline for the management of borderline personality disorder)
source_refs: National Health and Medical Research Council: Clinical practice guideline for the management of borderline personality disorder

options.text: Admit her to the psychiatric unit for a period of safety and daily review there
options.rationale: Inpatient admission for this presentation is associated with escalating self injury, regression and prolonged stays, which is precisely the pattern her own two previous admissions followed. It is reserved for a comorbid depressive or psychotic episode or a sustained and serious suicidal crisis that cannot be managed in the community. (Source: National Health and Medical Research Council: Clinical practice guideline for the management of borderline personality disorder)
source_refs: National Health and Medical Research Council: Clinical practice guideline for the management of borderline personality disorder

options.text: Follow her existing crisis plan and arrange therapist contact within two days
options.rationale: Self injury in this disorder is usually an attempt to regulate unbearable affect rather than an attempt to die, and her distress has already settled with time, food and containment, so the intervention that helps is validating the distress, treating the wounds, and reactivating the plan her own therapist wrote with her. Bringing forward contact with the existing team maintains continuity, which is the single factor most associated with reduced self harm over time. (Source: National Health and Medical Research Council: Clinical practice guideline for the management of borderline personality disorder)
source_refs: National Health and Medical Research Council: Clinical practice guideline for the management of borderline personality disorder

options.text: Give a dose of quetiapine and review her again in the department in two hours
options.rationale: Sedation has a limited role for severe acute distress that does not settle, but she has already settled without it, and drug treatment is not recommended as routine management of this disorder or of its crises. Repeated as-needed sedation in the department establishes a pattern that is hard to unwind. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic

options.text: Discharge her with advice to attend her next scheduled session in three days
options.rationale: Discharge is right and admission is wrong, but sending her out with no contact arranged for three days abandons the highest risk window, which is the days immediately following an episode of self harm. The difference from the correct answer is the active bridging contact rather than the destination. (Source: National Health and Medical Research Council: Clinical practice guideline for the management of borderline personality disorder)
source_refs: National Health and Medical Research Council: Clinical practice guideline for the management of borderline personality disorder

explanation.summary: Borderline personality disorder carries a lifetime suicide rate of around one in twenty five, so the risk is real, but the evidence consistently shows that inpatient admission after an episode of non-suicidal self injury does not reduce that risk and frequently worsens short term behaviour through regression and reinforcement. Australian guidance therefore favours brief, structured, validating emergency contact with rapid return to the existing community treatment, and explicitly discourages both admission and routine drug treatment. The clinician's task is to distinguish the habitual pattern of affect regulating self injury from a superimposed depressive episode, a psychotic episode or a genuine suicidal crisis, since those do change the disposition. Attitudes matter measurably here: pejorative framing in the notes and in handover predicts worse engagement and more presentations. The strongest protective factor available in the emergency department is continuity, which means talking to the team that already knows her rather than starting a parallel plan.
key_points: Self injury in this disorder usually regulates affect rather than expressing intent to die
Admission after self injury does not reduce suicide risk and often escalates behaviour
Drug treatment is not recommended as routine management of the disorder or its crises
Reactivating the existing crisis plan and team preserves continuity
Look actively for a comorbid depressive or psychotic episode, which changes the plan
explanation.pearls: The days immediately after an episode of self harm carry the highest short term suicide risk of any point in the illness, so whatever the disposition, arrange an actual contact within forty eight hours rather than relying on an already scheduled appointment, and make it a named person rather than a service number.

sources.label: National Health and Medical Research Council: Clinical practice guideline for the management of borderline personality disorder
Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

subtopic_detail: Low mood and worthlessness in a woman with metastatic cancer whose prognosis is measured in weeks
stem:
You are the consultation liaison psychiatry registrar asked to see a 61 year old woman with metastatic pancreatic cancer on the palliative care ward. The treating team estimates her prognosis at four to eight weeks and has asked about depression.

She describes three weeks of low mood present every day and all day, and says nothing lifts it, including a visit from her grandchildren which she previously looked forward to and which she found she could not enjoy at all. She says she has always been the strong one in the family and is now nothing, and that everyone would be better off if it were over. Her attention is intact, she recalls the ward routine accurately and her mental state has not fluctuated across two assessments on different days. Her pain is well controlled on a stable opioid dose and her calcium and sodium are normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88 beats per minute, blood pressure 106/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 96 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Cachectic, alert and fully oriented, months of the year backwards completed without error, no asterixis, affect uniformly flat with no reactivity
data_table.Investigations: Corrected calcium 2.34 mmol/L (2.10-2.60), sodium 138 mmol/L (135-145), bilirubin 14 micromol/L (less than 20), haemoglobin 102 g/L (115-155)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Start sertraline 50 mg daily and review her mood in four weeks
options.rationale: A serotonin reuptake inhibitor is the standard choice for a depressive episode, but the four to six weeks it needs to work is most or all of her remaining life. Time to benefit, rather than efficacy, is what disqualifies it here. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Palliative Care)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Palliative Care

options.text: Start mirtazapine 15 mg at night and review her mood in four weeks
options.rationale: Mirtazapine is attractive in this setting because it also helps nausea, appetite and sleep, and it is a good choice when the prognosis is months. Its effect on mood still takes two to four weeks, which is the specific reason it loses to a faster acting agent when the prognosis is weeks. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Palliative Care)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Palliative Care

options.text: Refer for cognitive behavioural therapy and review her mood in four weeks
options.rationale: Psychological therapy retains a place in palliative care, but structured cognitive behavioural therapy requires a course of sessions and a level of energy and concentration she is unlikely to sustain. Dignity focused and meaning centred brief therapies are the ones adapted for this timeframe. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Palliative Care)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Palliative Care

options.text: Start methylphenidate in the morning and review her mood in three days
options.rationale: Pervasive anhedonia that persists through a visit she would normally enjoy, with worthlessness that is not proportionate to her illness, marks a depressive episode rather than sadness or demoralisation, and with a prognosis of weeks the treatment chosen must act within days. Psychostimulants improve mood, energy and opioid related sedation within two to three days, which is why they are recommended in this specific situation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Palliative Care)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Palliative Care

options.text: Start olanzapine 2.5 mg at night and review her mood in three days
options.rationale: Low dose olanzapine is used in palliative care for nausea and for hypoactive delirium, and delirium is the differential worth taking seriously in a cachectic inpatient, but her attention is intact, she has no fluctuation across two assessments and there is no asterixis or metabolic abnormality. Treating the wrong syndrome costs her the weeks she has. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Palliative Care)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Palliative Care

explanation.summary: Depression is present in roughly one in six patients with advanced cancer and is under-treated because the somatic criteria that usually support the diagnosis, such as fatigue, anorexia and weight loss, are all produced by the disease itself. The cognitive and affective criteria carry the diagnostic weight instead: pervasive anhedonia that does not lift for anything, worthlessness or guilt out of proportion to circumstances, hopelessness that extends beyond the prognosis, and a wish to die that is not simply a wish for the dying to be over. Demoralisation, with loss of meaning and purpose but preserved capacity for pleasure, and hypoactive delirium, with inattention and fluctuation, are the two conditions most often mistaken for it and both require different treatment. When the prognosis is months, standard antidepressants are used, and mirtazapine is often favoured for its effect on nausea, appetite and sleep. When the prognosis is weeks, psychostimulants are recommended because they act within days, and they also counteract opioid induced sedation.
key_points: Somatic criteria are unreliable in advanced cancer; use the cognitive and affective ones
Pervasive anhedonia that does not lift for anything is the most useful single sign
Demoralisation preserves the capacity for pleasure; hypoactive delirium has inattention
Prognosis of months favours a standard antidepressant such as mirtazapine
Prognosis of weeks favours a psychostimulant because benefit appears within days
explanation.pearls: The single most discriminating question in this population is whether anything at all still gives pleasure, even briefly: preserved reactivity to a grandchild or a favourite piece of music points to demoralisation or sadness, while a complete and unbroken loss of that capacity in someone with intact attention points to a depressive episode worth treating within days.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists
